scope: All 7 origin paragraphs and all 16 complete accepted target paragraphs read; selected Hebrew, English and explanations compared in context. Original rejection ledger retained, with its previous full-reading evidence.
decision: Approve all 16 connections after four minor English fidelity/idiom repairs. No Hebrew, reference or fingerprint changed.

corrections.before: The beginning of words of Torah is desire, as it says, ‘His desire is in the Torah of the Lord.’ Then it is called the Lord’s Torah, as in Avodah Zarah 19a; afterwards comes attainment, called ‘and in his Torah he meditates.’ Desire is greater, as I heard concerning ‘A good name is better than good oil’ and the Sages’ saying that serving [Torah scholars] is greater [than studying]. Nevertheless, this is at the beginning and in youth, when desire is strong. Thus the end of Shabbat praises youth and describes old age, when desire is extinguished, unfavorably. Yet the Sages also praise aged Torah scholars, and elders are praised elsewhere. In truth they said, ‘I learned much from my teachers … and from my students more …’. ‘From my teachers’ refers to the beginning and desire. After the teacher’s passing, when it is called ‘his Torah’ because he toils himself to teach others, he then learns more and increases wisdom. Attainment, however, comes from God, for ‘the Lord gives wisdom,’ and everything is in Heaven’s hands except fear of Heaven. The latter is the receptive, feminine attribute and the awakening from below through desire and will; it is in the person’s hands, and therefore is good and great.
corrections.after: The beginning of words of Torah is desire, as it says, ‘His desire is in the Torah of the Lord.’ Then it is called the Lord’s Torah, as in Avodah Zarah 19a; afterwards comes attainment, called ‘and in his Torah he meditates.’ Desire is greater, as I heard concerning ‘A good name is better than good oil’ and the Sages’ saying that serving [Torah scholars] is greater [than studying]. corrections.before: At first God illuminates for a person. The person is not yet accustomed to this, finds it difficult to receive it as a peg fixed in a secure place that will not move, and loses it. Afterwards the person yearns after it and seeks it, but God does not reopen it for him except with great difficulty, as in ‘When I wanted, you did not want; now …’. This is the giving of Torah under the mountain held over them like a tub, followed by their accepting it again willingly in Ahasuerus’s days. Yet no miracle was performed for them in Ezra’s days as in Joshua’s, because the earlier sin caused this, and the Divine Presence did not dwell in the Second Temple. Nevertheless, the end of Sefer Heikhalot says that although Torah had been given, its seventeen listed qualities were not present until the Second Temple, even though the Divine Presence did not dwell there. It further says that they did not set stone upon stone in the Second Temple until they compelled the Holy One to reveal the secrets of everything. This ‘compulsion’ corresponds to the mountain’s compulsion at the giving of Torah. One may suggest that this compulsion was the removal of the evil inclination described in Yoma 69b, contrary to God’s will, as in ‘and that which I caused to be evil,’ and as I explained elsewhere.
corrections.after: At first God illuminates for a person. The person is not yet accustomed to this, finds it difficult to receive it as a peg fixed in a secure place that will not move, and loses it. corrections.before: ‘These are Noah’s generations … Make yourself an ark of gopher wood …’. The ark means that God gave Noah counsel and protection until the days of wrath had passed. Likewise anyone whose heart is not yet refined can learn counsels for sheltering himself and protecting himself from all the evil stirring in the world. Thus the Sages said: if a person sees sufferings coming upon him, let him run to the innermost chambers of Torah, and it gives him counsel for escape. The ark’s meaning follows the Talmud’s saying that the Holy One loves three: one who does not become angry, one who does not become drunk, and one who passes over his own measures. One who does not become angry does not show anger in action. One who does not become drunk possesses a settled mind and recognizes and believes in the Creator of the world. One who passes over his own measures removes anger even from his heart, so that no grievance against his fellow remains in his heart.
corrections.after: ‘These are Noah’s generations … Make yourself an ark of gopher wood …’. The ark means that God gave Noah counsel and protection until the days of wrath had passed. corrections.before: ‘In the third month after the children of Israel left Egypt … they encamped in the wilderness, and Israel encamped there opposite the mountain.’ My holy grandfather explained that desert travelers ordinarily camp beneath a mountain so that it protects them from winds and heat, with their faces looking toward the world. Here it says, ‘Israel encamped there opposite the mountain’: their backs faced the world and their faces the mountain. Their whole purpose was directed toward the mountain where they were to receive Torah. They did not wish to look toward worldly matters; they stood ready to receive Torah. Therefore it says, ‘Israel encamped,’ which Rashi, following the Mekhilta, explains as all being like one person with one heart. Division grows when a person turns toward worldly matters. Here, because they did not wish to look toward worldly matters, there was no division among them: they were like one person with one heart. This is what we say in the Haggadah: had He brought us near Mount Sinai without giving us Torah, it would have been enough. What good would there have been in coming near Sinai without receiving Torah? Through that very approach, before receiving Torah, Israel was clarified as not wishing to look toward worldly matters but only to hear what God would command them.
